extracted.intended_audience: AI/NLP researchers and practitioners building computational humor systems (vision-language, generative models) and HCI researchers evaluating humor generation
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating an AI system that generates humorous Instagram image captions targeted to Gen Z, including vision-language components, ideation, generation, fine-tuning, and human-subject evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-like skills for humor generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires a complex set of human skills: cognitive reasoning, social understanding, a broad base of knowledge, creative thinking, and audience understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper frames these as necessary capabilities to give to AI so it can write humor that resonates; they are invoked throughout system design and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes are often clever and require constructing facts to bring out absurdities, contradictions, and surprises — not just stating the obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive skills include logical manipulation of facts, multi-step reasoning, and constructing plausible but surprising inferences (e.g., semantic-script flips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding people, relationships, social norms, and what is socially appropriate to make fun of is necessary for effective humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes recognizing in-group knowledge, sensitivities, and benign-violation boundaries; used to pick targets and avoid overly threatening or inappropriate jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad base of knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A wide cultural and topical knowledge base enables making analogies, references, and associations that make jokes relatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For this system, Gen Z cultural touchstones (e.g., Minecraft, Snapchat, GTA) are important; fine-tuning increases coverage of target references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative thinking (divergent and convergent stages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor generation benefits from divergent exploration of many angles followed by convergent selection of the best punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors explicitly adopt an observation → divergent ideation → generation → ranking pipeline and say to 'favor quantity and diversity over quality' during ideation (generate many alternatives then narrow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience understanding / alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor must align with the tastes, slang, and reference points of the intended audience (here, Gen Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use target-audience data for fine-tuning and an audience-specific ranking model (Gen-Z humor agent) to filter and select outputs that match audience relatability and preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes should be relatable: listeners need to empathize or recognize the experience invoked by the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relatability can come from in-group references, shared experiences (work, school, relationships), and narratives that map the image onto common Gen Z conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational detail and specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Good jokes often arise from noticing non-obvious details and making sharp observations about the image or situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual Detail Extraction explicitly seeks 'non-obvious observations' (objects, expressions, background elements) as fodder for humor; avoid fixating on irrelevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative and point-of-view
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often contain narrative structure and a point of view (e.g., adopting someone's voice or an unexpected perspective) to reframe the setup and enable a surprising punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The system generates narratives/conflicts (e.g., 'Group Project Disaster', 'Tackling student loans') and uses them to create narrative-driven captions that map the image to a relatable story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise / benign violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor depends on violating expectations in a way that is surprising but not too threatening — the benign violation theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design captions that flip an inferred script or interpretation of the image (setup → punchline) to produce a second, unexpected interpretation consistent with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and diversity of strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce a mix of image-focused captions and narrative-driven captions, and ensure diversity to avoid predictability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate two types of captions (visual and narrative); ideation should yield many angles (authors generate 30 captions, then rank) because similar jokes lose surprise quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Detail Extraction (system component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Automatically produce a detailed paragraph describing who/what/where in the image, distinguishing subject, main action, and background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informs downstream ideation; examples: identify expressions, objects, background elements; explicit prompt to VLM to surface non-obvious visual elements for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Humor Ideation (system component)
rubrics_metrics.description: From extracted visual details, ideate on possible humorous visual elements (funny facial expressions, visual contrasts, metaphors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prompts to ask the model for humorous visual elements and metaphors (e.g., David vs. Goliath contrast) to seed caption generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative and Conflict Extrapolation (system component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generate narratives that reflect the essence of the image but map it into common, relatable experiences (work, school, relationships) to broaden joke targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain visual details + visual ideation + list of common Gen Z experiences to produce multiple narratives (authors show examples like 'Tackling student loans'). This expands humorous possibilities beyond literal image content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humorous caption generation process
rubrics_metrics.description: Given angles/narratives, generate many caption candidates (authors generate 15 visual-focused and 15 narrative-driven captions per image).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a fine-tuned generator for target style (GPT-3.5 fine-tuned on Gen Z Instagram comments); separate prompts for with/without narrative input; favor high quantity then filter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption ranking and filtering by audience agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a fine-tuned LLM (Gen-Z humor agent) to rank generated captions based on humor, relatability, and alignment with the image and narrative, returning the top-k (authors return top 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filter out captions that 'fail to meet the humor threshold' or are less relevant (example anti-pattern: captions that use Gen Z phrases but are not relatable to the image).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine-tuning on target-audience comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine-tune generation/evaluation models on a small dataset of high-quality, target-audience comments (authors used 80 humorous comments from popular IG meme pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include visual description + explanation of humorous elements in fine-tuning prompts so models learn style, tone, slang, and what targets resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of upvotes as human-ground-truth baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Top upvoted Instagram comments are used as a human baseline for what the audience finds funny (authors collect top-5 comments per post).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat upvotes as a proxy for audience approval/funniness when selecting human-composed comparators in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human evaluation with 1–5 funniness scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect human ratings of caption funniness on a 1 (not funny) to 5 (very funny) scale; raters drawn from the target audience and blind to condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomize image and caption order per participant, do not tell raters which captions are AI or human, and recruit participants matching the target demographic (authors recruited self-identified Gen Z who like Instagram caption humor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design controls (randomization and blinding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomize the order of images and captions, and blind raters to caption condition to avoid ordering and demand effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors randomized image order and caption order per image and kept condition labels hidden from participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis and significance testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use appropriate statistical models (authors used a Generalized Linear Mixed Model (GLMM)) with fixed effects for caption type and random effects for image ID and rater ID to assess differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report coefficients, standard errors, p-values, confidence intervals; account for ordinal nature of ratings and nested/random factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Out-of-domain generalization testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate system performance on non-target image domains (camera roll, museum art) to measure generalizability beyond Instagram meme images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generate captions for images from other datasets (Flickr, MoMA, The Met) and collect separate human ratings to compare against baseline models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cultural slang and insider references appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate audience-specific slang and cultural references (e.g., Gen Z slang like 'ahh', references to Minecraft, Snapchat, GTA) to increase resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fine-tuning helps replicate slang; ensure references map clearly to image content or generated narrative to avoid confusing non-insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fixation on irrelevant visual details (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline models sometimes 'drift towards non-significant visual details and fixate on them' rather than surfacing the most humor-relevant anomalies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design visual ideation to prioritize oddities/contrast/metaphor-worthy elements rather than mundane aspects (authors use Visual Detail Extraction to mitigate this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and punchiness as a quality factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, sharp captions can be especially effective (authors cite short IG captions as examples of high-rated comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, prefer succinct wording that delivers the punchline quickly; examples of successful short captions were highlighted in qualitative analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection and logical coherence check
rubrics_metrics.description: Generated jokes should be checked for logical sense: avoid outputs that are 'not logical enough to make sense, but also not illogical enough to be absurd' (these sound like mistakes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors suggest a reflection step (AI evaluating its own outputs) to think through the logic of a joke and filter nonsensical but non-absurd captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset/image selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Instagram Caption Challenge images tend to be interesting/unusual and often include people interacting; such images are more amenable to caption humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting images that already have interesting or unusual content increases the probability of producing good captions; images without people or obvious subjects (abstract art) are harder and require narrative extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations to be evaluated and reported
rubrics_metrics.description: Report constraints such as domain specificity (system fine-tuned for Gen Z Instagram captions), demographic limits of raters, and variability in humor ratings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that techniques may not generalize to other humor types (standup, magazine humor) and that insider/in-joke humor requires private/contextual data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation paradigms beyond prompt engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider multiple AI paradigms: prompt engineering, fine-tuning, chaining (chains-of-thought), reflection, agents, mixture-of-experts, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and RL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors describe their use of fine-tuning, chains, and a ranking agent, and recommend exploring other paradigms (reflection planning, RAG, human RL) for further gains.
